sections.title: Recognizing the species
sections.text: Ampulloclitocybe clavipes, also called clubfoot, has a grey-brown to ochre-brown cap, paler towards the margin. It begins convex with a small obtuse boss, then flattens and becomes depressed in the centre. The cream to pale yellow gills are crowded, sometimes forked, and strongly decurrent. The fibrous stem is similar in colour to the cap and broadens markedly into a club-shaped base.

sections.title: Flesh and useful characters
sections.text: The flesh is whitish and may be slightly yellow at the stem base; the centre can become soft and spongy. The smell is often mild or spicy, sometimes described as fruity, but varies between accounts. The spore print is white. The combination of the swollen stem base, decurrent gills and pale brown cap is more useful than any single character.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This saprotroph grows on soil and leaf or needle litter in broad-leaved and coniferous woodland, including beech and pine; it may also occur in open habitats. Fruiting is mainly from late summer through autumn, with timing varying by region.

sections.title: Alcohol and caution
sections.text: Reactions after alcohol consumption have been reported for this species. DGfM mentions an acetaldehyde-type syndrome, but coprine has not been detected in the cited medical sources and the mechanism remains uncertain; reported timing and symptoms are not consistent. Avoid combining it with alcohol as a precaution. Opinions on food value differ, and some references classify it as poisonous or suspect; this entry treats it as inedible.

traits: Grey-brown to ochre-brown cap, paler at the margin, convex then flattened and centrally depressed, sometimes with a small boss
Crowded cream to pale yellow gills, sometimes forked and strongly decurrent
Fibrous stem matching the cap, markedly swollen into a club-shaped base
Whitish flesh, sometimes yellowish at the stem base; variable mild or spicy smell; white spore print
Saprotroph on leaf or needle litter in broad-leaved and coniferous woodland · late summer and autumn
Reactions after alcohol have been reported; mechanism and symptoms vary, so avoid the combination
safetyNote: Treated as inedible. Reactions after alcohol have been reported, but coprine and a single mechanism have not been demonstrated; sources do not agree on timing or symptoms. Avoid combining with alcohol and do not eat this mushroom.
